package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability (CVE-2022-22965, 'SpringShell') that allows attackers to exploit data binding in the Spring framework. By sending specially crafted HTTP POST parameters, attackers can manipulate internal Java class properties to write arbitrary files (such as JSP webshells) to the server's webroot, resulting in full server compromise.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, upon receiving an HTTP POST request with crafted parameters

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
POST /path HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable-server
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern=%25%7B...malicious%20JSP%20code...%7D&class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.suffix=.jsp&class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.directory=webapps/ROOT&class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.prefix=shell&class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.fileDateFormat=
malicious_snippets.code_language: java (parameter binding exploit via HTTP POST)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the application processes an HTTP POST request, the data binder maps attacker-supplied parameters to internal Java class properties, enabling the writing of a malicious JSP file to the webroot directory, which results in remote code execution when accessed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code enables external HTTP POST parameters to directly modify internal Java class loader and file system properties, which is highly abnormal and allows attackers to write arbitrary files to sensitive locations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal data binding in Spring should only map user input to application-defined model objects, not to internal framework or class loader properties that control file writing or class loading.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate data binding is used for mapping form fields to user-defined POJOs (Plain Old Java Objects) for business logic, never for modifying internal Java class loader or file system properties.
key_indicators: Presence of HTTP POST parameters targeting class.module.classLoader.* properties
Ability to write arbitrary files (e.g., JSP webshells) to the webroot via parameter binding
Creation of new JSP files in Tomcat's webapps/ROOT directory
Parameter names such as class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.* in HTTP requests

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted HTTP POST request with parameters targeting internal class loader properties (e.g., class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern) to the vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: A malicious JSP file (webshell) is written to the webroot directory (e.g., webapps/ROOT/shell.jsp).

attack_chain.action: Attacker accesses the malicious JSP file via the web server, causing the server to execute the attacker's code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full server compromise through remote code execution (RCE).

behavioral_signatures: HTTP POST requests containing parameters with class.module.classLoader.*
Unexpected creation of JSP files in the webroot directory (e.g., webapps/ROOT/)
Parameter binding resulting in file creation outside of expected application logic
Access to newly created JSP files shortly after suspicious POST requests
file_indicators: Unexpected JSP files appearing in Tomcat webroot (webapps/ROOT/)
JSP files with suspicious or generic names (e.g., shell.jsp, cmd.jsp) created at unusual times
network_indicators: Unusual HTTP POST requests with class.module.classLoader.* parameters
Subsequent HTTP GET requests to newly created JSP files in the webroot
Spike in POST requests with parameter names not used by the legitimate application
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor HTTP POST requests for parameters matching class.module.classLoader.*. Alert on the creation of new JSP files in the webroot directory (webapps/ROOT/). Correlate suspicious POST requests with subsequent access to those files. Use software composition analysis (SCA) tools to flag deployments using vulnerable Spring versions (<5.3.18, <5.2.20). Implement file integrity monitoring on webroot directories to detect unauthorized JSP file creation.
